questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: A clause has a subject and a verb. Which group of words is an independent clause that can stand alone as a sentence?
options: When the falcon flew over the dunes
Because the falcon was so hungry
Over the dunes in the early morning
The falcon flew over the dunes
questions.why: It has a subject (the falcon) and a verb (flew), and it makes sense by itself.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a subordinating conjunction, a word that starts a dependent clause? “We stayed inside because the wind was strong.”
options: stayed
because
inside
wind
questions.why: Because starts the dependent clause “because the wind was strong.”

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which group of words is a dependent clause? It has a subject and a verb, but it cannot stand alone.
options: Huda finished all of her homework
her homework on the table
finished quickly and neatly
after Huda finished her homework
questions.why: “After Huda finished her homework” has a subject and a verb, but it leaves you asking “What happened then?”

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: True or false: The group of words “Khalid packed his lunch” can stand alone as a sentence.
questions.why: It has a subject (Khalid) and a verb (packed) and is a complete thought, so it is an independent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Choose the word that starts a dependent clause and completes the sentence: Omar wore his jacket ____ the morning was cold.
options: because
so
or
questions.why: Because tells the reason Omar wore his jacket.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: In the sentence “When the bell rang, the students lined up,” which part is the independent clause?
options: When the bell rang
When the bell rang, the
the students lined up
the bell rang, the students
questions.why: “The students lined up” can stand alone as a sentence.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Is each group of words an independent clause or a dependent clause?

rows.text: Sara read a story
while Sara read a story
the kitten slept on the rug
if the kitten wakes up

questions.why: Words like while and if turn a clause into a dependent clause that cannot stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence has a dependent clause?
options: Noura saw the gift on the kitchen table.
Noura and her sister saw the gift.
Noura saw the gift and smiled.
Noura smiled when she saw the gift.
questions.why: “When she saw the gift” is a dependent clause: it has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the dependent clause in this sentence about dinner.

segments.text: Before we ate dinner,
we washed our hands
with soap and water.

questions.why: “Before we ate dinner” starts with before and cannot stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which word can begin a dependent clause?
options: and
but
although
or
questions.why: Although is a subordinating conjunction. And, but and or join two independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which group of words needs another part to be a complete sentence?
options: If it rains tomorrow
It rained all day
The rain stopped at noon
We played after the rain
questions.why: “If it rains tomorrow” is a dependent clause. It needs an independent clause, such as “we will stay home.”

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: What does the dependent clause tell in this sentence? “We went to the park after the sun set.”
options: why we went to the park
how far away the park was
when we went to the park
who went to the park
questions.why: “After the sun set” tells when.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which two groups of words are dependent clauses? Choose two.
options: because the bus was late
the bus was late
the game ended at six
until the game ended
questions.why: Because and until make these clauses dependent. The other two can stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: Faisal could not play outside ____ he finished his chores.
options: and
or
until
questions.why: Until starts a dependent clause that tells when Faisal could play.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence is made of only one independent clause and nothing else?
options: My brother fed the goats before he left.
My older brother fed the hungry goats in the yard.
When the goats were hungry, my brother fed them.
My brother fed the goats because they were hungry.
questions.why: It has one subject and one verb and no dependent clause. The others each add a dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the subordinating conjunction in the sentence.

segments.text: The baby
slept
while
her mother
cooked rice.

questions.why: While starts the dependent clause “while her mother cooked rice.”

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which pair of words can both start a dependent clause?
options: although, and
unless, or
since, unless
but, yet
questions.why: Since and unless are subordinating conjunctions. The others are coordinating conjunctions.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Does each sentence have a dependent clause?

rows.text: Lama drew a picture of a palm tree.
Lama drew a palm tree while she waited.
If you water the plant, it will grow.
The plant grew tall and green.

questions.why: “While she waited” and “If you water the plant” are dependent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which clause best completes the sentence so that it makes sense? “________, we opened the windows.”
options: Because the room was cold
Because the room was quiet
Because the room was hot
The room was very hot
questions.why: A hot room is a good reason to open windows, and because makes the clause dependent. “The room was very hot” would need a joining word.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: True or false: Every dependent clause has a subject and a verb.
questions.why: All clauses have a subject and a verb. A dependent clause just cannot stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Which sentence is complex?
options: Since it was Friday, we visited our grandparents.
It was Friday, and we visited our grandparents.
We visited our grandparents on Friday after school.
It was Friday, so we visited our grandparents.
questions.why: “Since it was Friday” is a dependent clause joined to the independent clause “we visited our grandparents.”

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence uses a comma correctly after a dependent clause?
options: When the game ended the fans, cheered loudly.
When the game ended, the fans cheered loudly.
When, the game ended the fans cheered loudly.
When the game, ended the fans cheered loudly.
questions.why: When a dependent clause comes first, put a comma right after it.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Choose the word that makes this a complex sentence and shows contrast: ____ the test was hard, Yousef did not give up.
options: Although
Because
And
questions.why: Although shows that Yousef kept going even though the test was hard.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which part of this complex sentence is the dependent clause? “The children laughed when the clown fell down.”
options: The children laughed
The children laughed when
laughed when the clown
when the clown fell down
questions.why: “When the clown fell down” has a subject and verb but cannot stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: How can you join these two sentences into one complex sentence? “The shop was closed. We bought bread somewhere else.”
options: Because the shop was closed, we bought bread somewhere else.
The shop was closed, we bought bread somewhere else.
The shop was closed and, we bought bread somewhere else.
Because the shop was closed we, bought bread somewhere else.
questions.why: Because makes the first idea a dependent clause, and a comma follows it.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Read the sentences about a school trip. Which two are complex sentences? Choose two.
options: We sang songs while the bus drove to Taif.
The bus was big and blue.
After we arrived, the guide met us at the gate.
We saw roses, and we smelled them.
questions.why: Each complex sentence has a dependent clause (while…, after…). The others are simple or compound.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the word that joins the dependent clause to the rest of the sentence.

segments.text: Dana
kept
reading
until
the lights went out.

questions.why: Until is the subordinating conjunction that begins the dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence is NOT a complex sentence?
options: Majed smiled after he kicked the ball.
Majed kicked the ball, and it flew into the net.
If Majed kicks the ball hard, it will fly very far.
Before Majed kicked the ball, he took a breath.
questions.why: It joins two independent clauses with and, so it is compound. The others have a dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: True or false: “The library opens at eight, and it closes at two.” is a complex sentence.
questions.why: Both clauses can stand alone and are joined by and, so it is a compound sentence.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which of these words shows time when it starts a dependent clause?
options: because
before
although
unless
questions.why: Before tells when something happens. Because gives a reason, although shows contrast and unless shows a condition.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Where does the comma belong in this sentence? “If you finish early you may read a book.”
options: after early
after finish
after may
after read
questions.why: The dependent clause “If you finish early” comes first, so the comma goes right after it.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Is each sentence simple or complex?

rows.text: The kite rose high into the sky.
The kite rose high because the wind was strong.
Unless the wind blows, the kite will fall.
Turki and Salman flew the red kite.

questions.why: Complex sentences have a dependent clause starting with words like because or unless.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which dependent clause tells why?
options: when the road was flooded
because the road was flooded
where the road ends at the sea
after the road was fixed
questions.why: Because gives a reason. The others tell when or where.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence correctly joins these ideas with “although”? The water was cold. Bader swam in the sea.
options: Although the water was cold, but Bader swam in the sea.
Although the water was cold, Bader swam in the sea.
Although the water was cold. Bader swam in the sea.
The water was cold although, Bader swam in the sea.
questions.why: Use although to start the dependent clause, then a comma. Do not add but.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the complex sentence: ____ you heat ice, it melts into water.
options: But
When
So
questions.why: When starts a dependent clause that tells the time something happens.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this complex sentence.
questions.why: “When the oven was hot” cannot stand alone, so it needs a comma, not a period.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: In which sentence does the dependent clause come at the end?
options: As the team scored, we cheered loudly.
We cheered loudly as the team scored.
When we cheered, the team scored again.
If the team scores, we will cheer.
questions.why: “As the team scored” comes after the independent clause, so no comma is needed.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the sentence that is complex.

segments.text: Grandfather planted a lemon tree.
He watered it every morning.
When the first lemon grew, he gave it to me.

questions.why: “When the first lemon grew” is a dependent clause joined to an independent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which word should fill the blank to show a condition? “You can join the club ____ you bring a signed form.”
options: if
although
while
and
questions.why: If shows a condition: you can join only when you bring the form.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which two words could start the dependent clause in this sentence? “____ the sun set, the family ate dinner.” Choose two.
options: And
After
So
When
questions.why: After and when are subordinating conjunctions that tell time. And and so cannot start this clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence is a compound sentence, with two independent clauses joined by a word like and, but or so?
options: The museum was busy, so we came back later.
The museum was busy when we arrived.
Because the museum was busy, we left.
The busy museum had many visitors on Saturday.
questions.why: “The museum was busy” and “we came back later” can each stand alone, and so joins them.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Which sentence is compound-complex?
options: Ali rode his bike to the shop, and Sara walked the dog.
When the rain finally stopped, Ali rode his bike to the park.
Ali rode his bike after the rain stopped and the sun came out.
When the rain stopped, Ali rode his bike, and Sara walked the dog.
questions.why: It has one dependent clause (When the rain stopped) and two independent clauses joined by and.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Sort each sentence about Hessa's art class by its type.

rows.text: Hessa painted a vase.
Hessa painted a vase, and her sister made a bowl.
Hessa painted a vase while her sister made a bowl.

questions.why: Simple: one clause. Compound: two independent clauses. Complex: one independent clause and a dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: How many independent clauses are in this sentence? “Although it was late, Nada finished her project, and she showed it to her father.”
options: two
one
three
none
questions.why: “Nada finished her project” and “she showed it to her father” can each stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: What kind of sentence is this? “The cat hid under the bed because the thunder was loud.”
options: simple
compound
compound-complex
complex
questions.why: It has one independent clause and one dependent clause (because the thunder was loud).

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: True or false: A compound sentence must have a dependent clause.
questions.why: A compound sentence joins independent clauses. A sentence with a dependent clause is complex or compound-complex.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which two sentences are compound-complex? Choose two.
options: After the bell rang, the boys ran outside, and the girls went to the library.
We wanted to swim, but the pool was closed because it was being cleaned.
The boys ran outside after the bell rang.
We wanted to swim, but the pool was closed.
questions.why: Each correct sentence has two independent clauses and a dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence is simple?
options: My grandmother waters the mint, and she picks a few leaves.
Every morning, my grandmother waters the mint in her garden.
When the sun rises, my grandmother waters the mint.
My grandmother waters the mint so that it stays fresh and green.
questions.why: It has only one clause. “Every morning” and “in her garden” are phrases, not clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Choose the word that turns this into a compound-complex sentence: ____ the guests arrived, Mom served dates, and Dad poured coffee.
options: When
And
But
questions.why: When adds a dependent clause to the two independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the dependent clause in this compound-complex sentence.

segments.text: Ziyad studied hard,
and he passed the test
because he reviewed every night.

questions.why: “Because he reviewed every night” cannot stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: What type of sentence is this? “Layan wanted to buy a book, but she did not have enough money.”
options: simple
complex
compound
compound-complex
questions.why: Two independent clauses are joined by but, and there is no dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: What type of sentence is this? “If we leave early, we can see the camels, and we can still be home by noon.”
options: compound-complex
compound
complex
simple
questions.why: “If we leave early” is dependent, and two independent clauses are joined by and.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a coordinating conjunction that joins two independent clauses? “While the soup cooked, Maha set the table, and Fahad cut the bread.”
options: While
set
and
cut
questions.why: And joins “Maha set the table” and “Fahad cut the bread.” While starts the dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Is each sentence complex or compound-complex?

rows.text: The birds sang when the sun came up.
The birds sang when the sun came up, and the flowers opened.
Because it was windy, the door slammed shut.
Because it was windy, the door slammed, and the papers flew.

questions.why: Adding a second independent clause to a complex sentence makes it compound-complex.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence has exactly one independent clause and two dependent clauses?
options: The team won the match, and everyone cheered loudly.
When the team won, everyone cheered, and the coach smiled.
When the team won, we cheered because the match was close.
The team won the match and the shiny silver cup.
questions.why: “We cheered” is the only independent clause. “When the team won” and “because the match was close” are dependent.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about the guests.
questions.why: Two independent clauses need a comma and a joining word such as and.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which complex sentence tells what will happen on a condition?
options: It might rain later, so we will eat our lunch inside.
We had lunch in the garden with our cousins yesterday.
Unless it rains, we will have lunch in the garden.
It rained, but we ate in the garden.
questions.why: Unless sets a condition, and it starts a dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which two sentences have a dependent clause? Choose two.
options: Omar was tired, so he went to bed early.
Since Omar was tired, he went to bed early.
The cake that Grandma baked smelled wonderful.
Grandma baked a cake, and it smelled wonderful.
questions.why: “Since Omar was tired” and “that Grandma baked” are dependent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which change would make this simple sentence complex? “The children played football.”
options: Add a word such as “happily” after played.
Add another clause such as “and they had fun.”
Add a clause such as “after they finished lunch.”
Change football to “football and basketball.”
questions.why: Adding a dependent clause (after they finished lunch) makes the sentence complex.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the sentence that is compound-complex.

segments.text: The wind blew hard all night.
The tent shook, but it did not fall.
When morning came, we packed up, and we drove home.

questions.why: It has a dependent clause (When morning came) and two independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which choice correctly combines these sentences into one complex sentence? “The boy won the spelling bee. He lives next door.”
options: The boy who lives next door won the spelling bee.
The boy won the spelling bee, he lives next door.
The boy lives next door, and he won the spelling bee.
The boy, he lives next door, won the spelling bee.
questions.why: “Who lives next door” is a dependent clause that describes the boy.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence about meeting an uncle at the airport is compound-complex?
options: The plane landed late, so we waited at the gate for a long time.
We waited at the gate until our uncle finally came out with his bags.
The plane landed late, so we waited at the gate until our uncle came out.
Our uncle came out after the plane landed late.
questions.why: Two independent clauses (joined by so) plus the dependent clause “until our uncle came out.”

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Read the sentence. “The scientist, who studies desert plants, gave a talk, and the students asked many questions.” What makes it compound-complex?
options: It has one independent clause and two dependent clauses.
It has two independent clauses and no dependent clause.
It has three dependent clauses and no independent clause.
It has two independent clauses and one dependent clause.
questions.why: “The scientist gave a talk” and “the students asked many questions” are independent. “Who studies desert plants” is dependent.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Sort each sentence about Jana's poem by its type.

rows.text: Jana read the poem aloud.
Jana read the poem aloud, and the class clapped.
When Jana read the poem aloud, the class clapped.
When Jana read the poem, the class clapped, and the teacher smiled.

questions.why: Count the independent and dependent clauses in each sentence.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes the complex sentence: The museum ____ we visited has a dinosaur skeleton.
options: who
when
that
questions.why: That begins a clause that describes a thing (the museum). Who is used for people.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which revision turns this compound sentence into a compound-complex sentence? “The market was crowded, but we found fresh figs.”
options: The market was crowded, but we found fresh figs and sweet dates.
The market was crowded, so we found fresh figs.
The crowded market had fresh figs and dates for every shopper.
The market was crowded, but we found fresh figs before they sold out.
questions.why: Adding the dependent clause “before they sold out” makes it compound-complex.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which two sentences are complex but not compound-complex? Choose two.
options: The phone rang while we were eating, so Dad answered it later.
The hike was long, but nobody complained.
The phone rang while we were eating.
Although the hike was long, nobody complained.
questions.why: A complex sentence has only one independent clause. The other two have two independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: How many dependent clauses are in this sentence? “When the alarm rang, Salman jumped out of bed, and he dressed quickly because he was late.”
options: two
one
three
none
questions.why: “When the alarm rang” and “because he was late” are dependent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the two independent clauses in this compound-complex sentence.

segments.text: Although the path was steep,
the hikers kept climbing,
and they reached the top
before the sun set.

questions.why: “The hikers kept climbing” and “they reached the top” can each stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence uses a dependent clause to show contrast?
options: Because Rakan was nervous, he practiced his speech.
Even though Rakan was nervous, he gave a clear speech.
Rakan practiced his speech for days until he knew it well.
After Rakan gave his speech, he sat down.
questions.why: Even though shows contrast: he was nervous, yet he spoke clearly.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which choice combines these three ideas into one compound-complex sentence? “The power went out. We lit candles. Grandfather told stories.”
options: The power went out, we lit candles, Grandfather told stories.
The power went out, and we lit candles and told old stories together.
We lit candles and listened to stories when the power went out.
When the power went out, we lit candles, and Grandfather told stories.
questions.why: It keeps all three ideas: one dependent clause and two independent clauses joined by and.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which compound-complex sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: Before the race began the runners stretched, and, the crowd took their seats.
Before the race began, the runners stretched the crowd took their seats.
Before the race began, the runners stretched, and the crowd took their seats.
Before, the race began, the runners stretched and the crowd, took their seats.
questions.why: Put a comma after the opening dependent clause and before and when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: True or false: “The students who finished early helped the others, and the teacher thanked them.” is a compound-complex sentence.
questions.why: “Who finished early” is a dependent clause, and there are two independent clauses joined by and.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Read the sentence. “Our class planted trees in the schoolyard because the principal asked us to help.” Which change would make it compound-complex?
options: Remove “because the principal asked us to help.”
Add “, and the trees grew quickly” at the end.
Change “because” to “and.”
Add “green” before “trees.”
questions.why: Adding a second independent clause to this complex sentence makes it compound-complex.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this compound-complex sentence.
segments: the bus took a longer way
for the start of the game.
questions.correction: the bus took a longer way,
questions.why: Put a comma before and when it joins two independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Is each clause from this sentence independent or dependent? “Although Ghada was tired, she finished her painting, and she hung it on the wall.”

rows.text: Although Ghada was tired
she finished her painting
she hung it on the wall

questions.why: Although makes the first clause dependent. The other two can stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which subordinating conjunction best shows that one event caused another? “____ the river flooded, the farmers moved their animals to higher ground.”
options: Although
Unless
Because
Whereas
questions.why: Because shows cause and effect: the flood made the farmers move their animals.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which is the best way to combine these sentences? “Ali found a wallet. He returned it to its owner. The owner thanked him.”
options: Ali found a wallet, he returned it, the owner thanked him.
Although Ali found a wallet, he returned it to its owner, and the owner thanked him.
After Ali found a wallet, he returned it to its owner, and the owner thanked him.
Ali found a wallet after he returned it to its owner and thanked him.
questions.why: After shows the right order of events, and the commas are correct.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which two clauses in this sentence are independent? “The bell rang before the test ended, but the teacher gave us extra time because the fire drill had stopped us.” Choose two.
options: The bell rang
the teacher gave us extra time
before the test ended
because the fire drill had stopped us
questions.why: Before and because start dependent clauses. The other two clauses can stand alone.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence has a dependent clause that describes a noun?
options: Huda wrote a poem, and it won first prize.
The poem that Huda wrote won first prize.
Huda smiled when her poem won first prize.
Because her poem won, Huda smiled.
questions.why: “That Huda wrote” tells which poem, so it describes the noun poem.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which revision best shows that the second event happened in spite of the first? “The test was difficult. Most students passed it.”
options: Although the test was difficult, most students passed it.
Because the test was difficult, most students passed it.
The test was difficult, so most students passed it.
When the test was difficult, most of the students passed it.
questions.why: Although shows contrast: students passed even though the test was hard.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence about the new library is punctuated correctly?
options: The new library which opened last week, has a reading garden, and students love it.
The new library, which opened last week has a reading garden and, students love it.
The new library, which opened last week, has a reading garden students love it.
The new library, which opened last week, has a reading garden, and students love it.
questions.why: Extra information (which opened last week) needs a comma on both sides, and a comma comes before and.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly in a compound-complex sentence?
options: Because the flight was delayed, we waited for hours; however, the airline gave us snacks.
Because the flight was delayed; we waited for hours, however the airline gave us snacks.
Because; the flight was delayed, we waited for hours however the airline gave us snacks.
Because the flight was delayed, we waited; for hours, however, the airline gave us snacks.
questions.why: A semicolon joins the two independent clauses, and however is followed by a comma.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: A writer wants the main point, that the team won, to be in the independent clause. Which sentence does this best?
options: Although the team won the championship, two players were injured.
The team won, and two players were injured.
Two players were injured when the team won the championship.
Although two players were injured, the team won the championship.
questions.why: The most important idea belongs in the independent clause; the less important idea goes in the dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the clause that should be set off with commas because it adds extra information.

segments.text: My cousin Abdullah
who lives in Jeddah
is visiting us this week
and he brought gifts.

questions.why: We already know who Abdullah is, so “who lives in Jeddah” is extra and needs commas.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which compound-complex sentence is written correctly?
options: Whenever Dana reads before bed, she sleeps well, she wakes up early.
Whenever Dana reads before bed she sleeps well and, she wakes up early.
Whenever Dana reads before bed. She sleeps well, and she wakes up early.
Whenever Dana reads before bed, she sleeps well, and she wakes up early.
questions.why: It has a comma after the dependent clause and a comma plus and between the independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Sort each sentence about the match by its type.

rows.text: Feeling ready, the players walked onto the field.
The players had trained for weeks, yet they felt nervous.
Before the match, the players, who had trained for weeks, felt ready.
The players felt ready because they had trained, but the rain delayed the match.

questions.why: Phrases such as “Feeling ready” and “Before the match” are not clauses. Count only groups with a subject and a verb.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which subordinating conjunction makes the relationship between the clauses clearest? “____ the desert is very dry, some plants store water in their thick leaves.”
options: Unless
Because
Although
Until
questions.why: The dry desert is the reason the plants store water, so because fits best.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Read the sentence. “Since the museum was free on Saturday, many families visited, but the café ran out of food.” What is the job of the clause “Since the museum was free on Saturday”?
options: It tells when the café ran out of food.
It names the families who visited the museum.
It contrasts the museum with the café.
It gives a reason for the families’ visit.
questions.why: Here since means because, so the clause explains why many families visited.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Find and fix the error in this sentence about Noura's soup.
questions.why: A cold soup is not a reason to eat it all. Although shows the contrast the writer means.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which revision combines these ideas into a compound-complex sentence without changing the meaning? “The scouts reached the camp. It was dark. They set up their tents. They cooked dinner.”
options: After the scouts reached camp in the dark, they set up tents, and they cooked dinner.
The scouts reached the camp, it was dark, they set up tents, they cooked dinner.
The scouts reached the camp in the dark, set up their tents, and then cooked dinner.
Because the scouts set up their tents, it was dark when they reached the camp.
questions.why: It has one dependent clause and two independent clauses and keeps the order of events. The third choice is a simple sentence.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which of these sentences is compound-complex?
options: The girl who won the race thanked her coach, and her parents cheered.
The girl who won the race thanked her coach and her parents.
The girl thanked her coach and her parents after the race.
Winning the race, the girl thanked her coach, and her parents cheered.
questions.why: “Who won the race” is dependent, and two independent clauses are joined by and. “Winning the race” is only a phrase.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which two of these sentences about a family trip are compound-complex? Choose two.
options: The house that we rented was small, but it had a lovely view.
Having rented a small house, we enjoyed its lovely view.
We left early so that we would beat the traffic; nevertheless, we arrived late.
The small house had a lovely view, and we enjoyed it every day.
questions.why: Each correct sentence has two independent clauses and a dependent clause (that we rented, so that we would beat the traffic).

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Read the sentence. “Whoever finishes the puzzle first will win a prize, and everyone else will get a sticker.” Which part is the dependent clause?
options: will win a prize
Whoever finishes the puzzle first
everyone else will get a sticker
Whoever finishes the puzzle first will win a prize
questions.why: “Whoever finishes the puzzle first” is a dependent clause that acts as the subject of the first independent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which sentence starts with a dependent clause and keeps the meaning of “Fahad saved his money for months so he could buy a telescope”?
options: So that he could buy a telescope, Fahad saved his money for months.
Fahad, so he could buy a telescope, months saved his money.
Saving his money, Fahad bought a telescope for months.
For months, Fahad bought a telescope so that he could save his money.
questions.why: Moving the dependent clause to the front varies the sentence without changing its meaning.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Select the clause that is not independent.

segments.text: The mountains looked purple
as the sun went down,
and the air grew cool,
so we put on our jackets.

questions.why: As is a subordinating conjunction. And and so join independent clauses.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Choose the word that correctly completes this compound-complex sentence: The students wanted to stay longer ____ the exhibit was so interesting, but the bus was waiting.
options: and
because
so
questions.why: Because makes “the exhibit was so interesting” a dependent clause giving the reason.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: Which choice is the clearest and least wordy way to combine these sentences? “Reem entered the contest. The contest was for young writers. She wanted to share her story.”
options: Reem entered the contest, and the contest was for young writers, and she wanted to share her story.
Reem entered the contest, which was a contest that was for young writers, because she wanted to share her story.
Because Reem entered the contest for young writers, she wanted to share her story.
Reem entered the contest for young writers because she wanted to share her story.
questions.why: It is short, clear and shows the right reason. The last choice turns the cause and effect around.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: True or false: In the sentence “When the lights dimmed, the audience became quiet, and the play began,” the clause “the play began” is a dependent clause.
questions.why: “The play began” can stand alone, so it is independent. “When the lights dimmed” is the dependent clause.

questions.mapArea: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
questions.stem: A writer used many short sentences: “The wind howled. The tent flapped. We were scared. We stayed inside.” Which revision best varies them with one compound-complex sentence?
options: The wind howled, the tent flapped, we were scared, we stayed inside.
As the wind howled and the tent flapped, we were scared, but we stayed inside.
The wind howled and the tent flapped and we were scared and we stayed inside.
The wind howled. The tent flapped because we were scared. We stayed inside.
questions.why: It joins the ideas with a dependent clause (As…) and two independent clauses joined by but.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: I got a red bike for Eid. I rode it to my cousin's house. My cousin and I raced down the street. I won the race!
questions.stem: Who is telling this story about the red bike?
options: someone outside the story who uses he
the reader, who is called you
a character in the story who uses I
the cousin, who uses the word we
questions.why: The narrator says I and my, so the narrator is a character in the story.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Salma heard a tiny cry under the car. She bent down and saw a kitten. Salma gave it some milk. The kitten purred happily.
questions.stem: Which words in the kitten story tell you it is told in third person?
options: I, me, my
Salma, she, it
we, us, our
you, your, yours
questions.why: Third person uses names and words like she and it.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: First, you dig a small hole. Next, you drop in two seeds. Then you cover them with soil. Finally, you water them every day.
questions.stem: What point of view is used in these planting directions?
options: second person
first person
third person limited
third person omniscient
questions.why: The directions speak to the reader as you.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: We drove to the beach in Al Khobar. The water was warm and blue. I found a pink shell. The sand castles were tall.
questions.stem: Select the two sentences that show the narrator is part of the beach trip.

segments.text: We drove to the beach in Al Khobar.
The water was warm and blue.
I found a pink shell.
The sand castles were tall.

questions.why: We and I show that the narrator was there.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Omar opened his lunch box. He found a sandwich and an apple. He smiled because his mother had packed his favorite food.
questions.stem: Is the lunch box story told in first person or third person?
options: first person, because the narrator uses he and his
first person, because Omar is the main character
third person, because the narrator uses he and his
second person, because the story is about lunch
questions.why: He and his are third-person words. The narrator tells about Omar from outside.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: I kicked the ball as hard as I could. It flew past the goalkeeper. My team cheered, and I jumped high in the air.
questions.stem: True or false: The narrator of the football story is a character in the story.
questions.why: The narrator uses I and my team, so the narrator is in the story.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Every Friday, I visit my grandmother. Her kitchen smells like cardamom and fresh bread. She lets me help her make kleija cookies.
questions.stem: Which pronoun tells you this story about Grandmother's kitchen is told in first person?
options: I
she
her
they
questions.why: I is a first-person pronoun. The narrator is telling about himself or herself.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Is each sentence written in first person or third person?

rows.text: I fed the ducks at the park.
She fed the ducks at the park.
We watched the ducks swim.
They watched the ducks swim.

questions.why: I and we are first person. She and they are third person.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: You walk up to the desk. You hand the librarian your new card. She smiles and gives you your first book.
questions.stem: In the library card passage, who is the word you talking to?
options: the librarian
the narrator's friend
a character named You
the reader
questions.why: In second person, you speaks to the reader.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Choose the pronoun that keeps this sentence in first person: ____ packed my bag for the school trip.
options: She
I
You
questions.why: I matches my and shows the speaker is telling about himself or herself.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Lama looked out the window. Dark clouds covered the mountains. Lama hoped the rain would stop before her picnic. She crossed her fingers.
questions.stem: What point of view is the rain story told from?
options: first person
third person
second person
first person plural (we)
questions.why: The narrator tells about Lama using her name and she.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Our class had a science fair. I made a volcano with baking soda. My friend Reem made a solar oven. We all clapped when the judges came.
questions.stem: Which two words show that the science fair passage is told in first person? Choose two.
options: I
Reem
We
judges
questions.why: I and we are first-person pronouns used by the narrator.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: The camel walked across the hot sand. It carried water for the travelers. The travelers were thankful for the strong camel.
questions.stem: Who is telling the camel story?
options: a narrator outside the story
the strong camel in the story
one of the thankful travelers
the reader of the story
questions.why: No one in the story says I. The narrator tells about the camel and the travelers from outside.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Dad boiled water in the kettle. I added the tea leaves and a sprig of mint. Dad poured a cup for each of us.
questions.stem: How do you know the narrator is a character in the tea story?
options: The narrator uses the word I.
The narrator talks about Dad.
The story has tea and mint.
The narrator uses the word each.
questions.why: I shows the narrator is taking part in the story.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: The owl sat in the old tree. It closed its eyes all day long. At night, it flew over the farm to hunt.
questions.stem: Which word from the owl story is a third-person pronoun?
options: I
we
it
you
questions.why: It is a third-person pronoun. The narrator tells about the owl from outside.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: You hold the string tightly. You run into the wind. Your kite rises higher and higher!
questions.stem: Why is the kite passage told in second person?
options: It uses I and my to tell about the narrator.
It uses you and your to speak to the reader.
It uses he and his to tell about a boy.
It uses they and their to tell about kites.
questions.why: Second person speaks to the reader with you and your.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Is each sentence written in first, second, or third person?

rows.text: You should wear a hat in the sun.
My hat keeps the sun off my face.
His hat is blue and white.

questions.why: My is first person, you is second person and his is third person.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Sara and her brother saved their coins for a month. They bought a small plant for their mother. Mama hugged them both.
questions.stem: If Sara told this story herself, how would the first sentence begin?
options: Sara and her brother saved their coins for a month.
You and your brother saved your coins for a month.
They saved their coins for a month.
My brother and I saved our coins for a month.
questions.why: In first person, Sara would use I, my and our.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Khalid's uncle owns a date farm. Khalid helps pick the dates every summer. He likes the sweet, sticky ones best.
questions.stem: True or false: The date farm passage is told in first person because it tells what Khalid likes.
questions.why: The narrator uses Khalid's name and he, so it is third person.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Choose the pronoun that keeps this sentence in third person: Rakan finished ____ homework before dinner.
options: my
your
his
questions.why: His is a third-person pronoun that matches Rakan.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: I hid behind the couch with my cousins. When Aunt Hessa opened the door, we jumped up and shouted. She laughed so hard that she dropped her bag.
questions.stem: From which point of view is the surprise party story told?
options: first person
second person
third person limited
third person omniscient
questions.why: The narrator uses I and we and is part of the party.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Before you feed a goat, wash your hands. Hold the food flat on your palm. Keep your fingers together so the goat does not nibble them.
questions.stem: Which point of view does the writer of the goat-feeding tips use, and why?
options: first person, to tell about the writer's goat
third person, to tell a story about a farmer
second person, to give the reader directions
first person, to explain the writer's feelings
questions.why: The writer speaks to the reader as you to explain the steps.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Is the narrator of each sentence a character who takes part (first person) or someone outside the events (third person)?

rows.text: I could not believe my eyes when the door opened.
Faisal could not believe his eyes when the door opened.
We ran to the window to see the parade.
The children ran to the window to see the parade.

questions.why: A narrator who says I or we is in the story. A narrator who uses names and he or they is outside it.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Bader walked to the old well at the edge of the village. He dropped a pebble and listened. Plop! He wondered how deep the water was.
questions.stem: Which clue shows that the narrator of the well story is not a character in it?
options: The narrator calls Bader by name and uses he.
The narrator describes the old well in the village.
The narrator uses the sound word Plop!
The narrator tells where the well is.
questions.why: A narrator outside the story uses the character's name and he or she.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: We waited at the table as the sun went down. My little sister counted the dates on her plate. When we heard the call to prayer, I passed the water jug to my father.
questions.stem: Which two details show that the narrator is part of this evening scene? Choose two.
options: the sun went down
We waited at the table
the call to prayer
I passed the water jug
questions.why: We and I show the narrator is at the table.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: The parrot in the pet shop said hello to everyone. Children laughed whenever it whistled. The shop owner, Mr. Saleh, gave it a cracker each morning.
questions.stem: Which point of view does the narrator of the pet shop story use?
options: first person
second person
third person
first person plural
questions.why: The narrator tells about the parrot, the children and Mr. Saleh from outside.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: The sand was hot under my feet. Jana climbed quickly up the dune. She waved from the top of the dune. I took a deep breath and kept going.
questions.stem: Select the two sentences that use a first-person pronoun for the narrator.

segments.text: The sand was hot under my feet.
Jana climbed quickly up the dune.
She waved from the top of the dune.
I took a deep breath and kept going.

questions.why: My and I are first-person pronouns.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: You open the old wooden box. Inside, you find a map with a red X. Your heart beats fast as you wonder where it leads.
questions.stem: Which words show that the treasure box passage is in second person?
options: I, my
you, your
he, his
they, their
questions.why: You and your speak straight to the reader.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: True or false: A story told in third person uses words like he, she and they for the characters.
questions.why: Third-person narrators use names and he, she, it and they.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Choose the word that puts this sentence in second person: ____ should always wear a seat belt in the car.
options: I
He
You
questions.why: You speaks directly to the reader.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Maha held her mother's hand in the busy souq. Then she stopped to look at a shiny bracelet. When she turned around, her mother was gone! Maha's heart pounded.
questions.stem: Who is the narrator of the souq passage?
options: Maha, who tells what happened to her in the souq
Maha's mother, who tells about her daughter
a narrator outside the story who tells about Maha
the shopkeeper, who sells Maha the shiny bracelet
questions.why: The narrator uses Maha's name and she, so the narrator is outside the story.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Dad and I sailed out at sunrise. I held the fishing line for an hour, and nothing happened. Then something tugged so hard that I almost fell! Dad laughed and helped me pull in a big hamour.
questions.stem: What can the reader learn from the first-person narrator of the fishing story?
options: what Dad is secretly thinking the whole time
what the narrator does and feels during the trip
what the fish is thinking under the water
what every person on the beach is doing that day
questions.why: A first-person narrator can share only his or her own actions and feelings.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Sort each sentence by its point of view.

rows.text: I hope it rains tomorrow.
You can see the stars from the roof.
Fahad hopes it rains tomorrow.
We all hope it rains tomorrow.

questions.why: I and we are first person, you is second person, and a name such as Fahad is third person.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Ziyad walked into the classroom on his first day. Twenty faces turned to look at him. Ziyad felt his cheeks get warm. He sat in the only empty chair.
questions.stem: If Ziyad were the narrator of the new student story, which sentence would be correct?
options: Ziyad felt his cheeks get warm.
I felt my cheeks get warm.
You felt your cheeks get warm.
He felt his cheeks get warm.
questions.why: If Ziyad told the story, he would use I and my.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: The sky turned orange. Khalid pulled his scarf over his nose. His sister Nada grabbed his arm. They hurried home before the storm hit.
questions.stem: Which two words in the sandstorm passage are third-person pronouns? Choose two.
options: his
They
sky
storm
questions.why: His and they are third-person pronouns. Sky and storm are nouns.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: You will need wood, nails and a hammer. First, you cut the wood into six pieces. Then you nail the pieces together. Ask an adult to help you with the hammer.
questions.stem: Why might the writer have chosen second person for the birdhouse steps?
options: to tell a story about a birdhouse the writer once built
to show the thoughts of every character
to speak directly to the reader who follows the steps
to describe a bird that lives in a birdhouse
questions.why: Second person (you) works well for directions a reader will follow.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Turki searched under his bed for his left shoe. His brother pretended to read a book. Turki noticed a shoelace peeking out from behind his brother's back. Turki laughed and grabbed it.
questions.stem: Select the sentence in which the narrator tells what Turki noticed.

segments.text: Turki searched under his bed for his left shoe.
His brother pretended to read a book.
Turki noticed a shoelace peeking out from behind his brother's back.
Turki laughed and grabbed it.

questions.why: The word noticed tells what Turki saw.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: We lined up at the starting line. My legs were shaking. When the whistle blew, I ran faster than I ever had before.
questions.stem: Which sentence would change the race story to third person?
options: When the whistle blew, Noura ran faster than she ever had before.
When the whistle blew, I ran faster than I ever had before.
When the whistle blew, you ran faster than you ever had before.
When the whistle blew, we ran faster than we ever had before.
questions.why: Third person uses a name and she instead of I.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: My uncle trained a falcon named Sahm. I watched him hold out his glove. The falcon swooped down and landed on it.
questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence: The narrator of the falcon story is ____.
options: a character who watches the uncle
someone outside the story
the falcon named Sahm
questions.why: The narrator says I watched, so the narrator is a character in the story.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: True or false: A first-person narrator can always tell exactly what every other character is thinking.
questions.why: A first-person narrator is one character, so he or she can only guess what others think.

sets.skill: Point of View: First, Second, Third Limited, Third Omniscient

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Yousef stood on the stage and stared at the judges. His hands were sweaty. He wondered if he could remember how to spell “necessary.” He took a deep breath and began.
questions.stem: Which point of view is used in the spelling bee passage?
options: third person omniscient
first person
second person
third person limited
questions.why: The narrator tells only Yousef's thoughts and feelings.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Huda knocked the vase off the shelf and felt terrible. In the next room, her mother heard the crash and worried that someone was hurt. Huda's little brother hid behind the door, afraid he would be blamed.
questions.stem: Why is the broken vase passage told in third person omniscient?
options: The narrator tells only Huda's thoughts and feelings about the vase.
The narrator tells the thoughts and feelings of several characters.
The narrator is Huda, who tells the story using I.
The narrator speaks directly to the reader using you.
questions.why: We learn how Huda, her mother and her brother each feel.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Read each description. Is it third person limited or third person omniscient?

rows.text: The narrator shares only one character's thoughts.
The narrator shares the thoughts of many characters.
The narrator knows what is happening in two different places.
The reader learns only what one character notices.

questions.why: Limited follows one character. Omniscient means all-knowing.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Sara spread the striped blanket under the tall palm tree. The sun was warm and bright over the quiet green park. She hoped her friends would like the sandwiches she had made. She did not know that Reem was planning a surprise cake.
questions.stem: Which sentence shows that the narrator of the picnic passage knows more than Sara does?
options: Sara spread the striped blanket under the tall palm tree.
She hoped her friends would like the sandwiches.
The sun was warm and bright over the quiet green park.
She did not know that Reem was planning a surprise cake.
questions.why: Sara does not know about the cake, but the narrator does.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Faisal frowned at his wobbly model of the solar system. He worried it would fall apart before the fair. Across town, his friend Majed felt proud of his finished robot. Majed thought winning would be easy.
questions.stem: Which two details show that the science project passage uses third person omniscient? Choose two.
options: Faisal's model was wobbly.
Faisal worried his model would fall apart.
Majed thought winning would be easy.
Majed's robot was finished.
questions.why: The narrator shares the private thoughts of two different boys.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Lama tapped her foot at the bus stop. The bus was late again. She wondered if she should walk to school instead. She checked the time and sighed.
questions.stem: Whose thoughts does the reader learn in the bus stop passage?
options: only the bus driver's
Lama's and the driver's
only Lama's
no one's
questions.why: The narrator follows only Lama, so it is third person limited.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Salman wanted the last piece of kunafa, but he said nothing. Rakan also wanted it, but he offered it to his brother. Salman felt grateful and decided to share.
questions.stem: True or false: The kunafa passage is told in third person limited because it tells about two brothers.
questions.why: It shows what both brothers want and feel, so it is third person omniscient.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Mrs. Al-Harbi watered her roses every morning. She secretly worried that her neighbor's garden was prettier. Next door, Mr. Al-Qahtani was sure his jasmine would win. The judges would arrive on Thursday.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Ali dribbled the ball toward the goal. The goalkeeper bent his knees, thinking Ali would kick to the left. Ali's coach held his breath on the side of the field, hoping for a goal.
questions.stem: What point of view does the football match passage use?
options: third person omniscient
third person limited
first person
second person
questions.why: The narrator tells what the goalkeeper thinks and what the coach hopes.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Choose the words that complete the sentence: A narrator who tells the thoughts of only one character is using ____.
options: third person limited
third person omniscient
second person
questions.why: Limited means the narrator stays with one character.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Tariq lay in the tent and listened to the wind. He was sure he heard footsteps outside. He pulled his blanket up to his chin. Was it a fox? Was it his cousin playing a trick?
questions.stem: Why does the author use third person limited in the desert camp passage?
options: to show what the fox outside is thinking and planning
to explain what every camper in the tent is feeling
to let the reader share Tariq's fear of the unknown sound
to speak to the reader as you, the one in the tent
questions.why: Because we know only what Tariq knows, we wonder about the sound too.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Noura searched every drawer for the key to her bicycle lock. Her father, reading in the next room, remembered that he had put it in his pocket that morning. Noura's younger brother knew too, but he was enjoying watching her search.
questions.stem: What does the omniscient narrator let the reader know that Noura does not know?
options: Noura is looking for the key to her bicycle lock.
Noura's father is reading in the next room.
Noura has searched every drawer in the whole house.
Her father and her brother both know where the key is.
questions.why: The narrator shares what her father and brother know.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Is each short passage third person limited or third person omniscient?

rows.text: Dana smiled. She hoped her friend would like the card.
Dana smiled, hoping her friend would like it. Her friend, Ghada, was thinking about a card of her own.
Omar ran home. He was afraid he had missed dinner.
Omar ran home, afraid he was late. His mother, at the window, was thinking that he was early.

questions.why: When the thoughts of a second character appear, the narrator is omniscient.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Mr. Fahad counted the students as they climbed onto the bus. He hoped no one would get lost at the museum. In the back row, Abdullah grinned; he planned to see the dinosaur room first, no matter what. Beside him, Sami was quietly nervous about the long ride.
questions.stem: Which detail best shows that the narrator of the class trip passage is omniscient?
options: The narrator tells that Mr. Fahad counted the students on the bus.
The narrator tells what three different people are thinking.
The narrator describes the students climbing onto the bus.
The narrator says Abdullah sat in the back row.
questions.why: An omniscient narrator can see into the minds of many characters.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Reem set out cups of cold lemonade. She thought the price was fair. A man walking by thought the lemonade looked too sour. A little girl wished she had brought her coins.
questions.stem: Which two sentences show the thoughts of characters other than Reem? Choose two.
options: A man walking by thought the lemonade looked too sour.
Reem set out cups of cold lemonade.
A little girl wished she had brought her coins.
She thought the price was fair.
questions.why: The narrator also shares what the man thinks and what the girl wishes.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Hessa walked onto the stage with her oud. She could hear her own heartbeat. She looked for her father in the crowd and finally spotted his proud smile.
questions.stem: If the recital passage were told in third person omniscient, what might the narrator add?
options: what Hessa could hear as she walked onstage
what Hessa's father was thinking as he watched her
how Hessa felt just before she started playing
where Hessa saw her father in the crowd
questions.why: An omniscient narrator could also share the father's thoughts.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Dark clouds gathered over the hill. The little ant hurried to carry one more seed to its nest. It feared the rain would wash the path away. Far above, a bird watched the ant and wondered why it worked so hard.
questions.stem: Select the sentence that shows the narrator is omniscient rather than limited to the ant.

segments.text: Dark clouds gathered over the hill.
The little ant hurried to carry one more seed to its nest.
It feared the rain would wash the path away.
Far above, a bird watched the ant and wondered why it worked so hard.

questions.why: The narrator also knows what the bird wonders.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Majed read the message on his phone three times. “Meet me at the park,” it said, but there was no name. He felt both curious and nervous. He grabbed his jacket and headed out the door.
questions.stem: Why can't the reader know who sent Majed the message?
options: It is first person, so the narrator chooses to hide the answer.
It is third person limited, so we know only what Majed knows.
It is third person omniscient, so every thought is shared.
It is second person, so the reader must be the one who sent it.
questions.why: A limited narrator stays with Majed, and Majed does not know.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Grandmother stirred the rice and smiled; she knew this was the children's favorite dish. In the living room, Jana was hoping dinner would be ready soon, while her brother wondered if there would be dessert.
questions.stem: True or false: The kabsa passage is told from a third person omniscient point of view.
questions.why: The narrator shares what Grandmother knows, what Jana hopes and what her brother wonders.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Yousef placed his paper boat in the stream. The water sparkled in the bright afternoon sun. He watched it float away and hoped it would reach the sea. He did not see the small rock waiting around the bend.
questions.stem: Which sentence tells the reader something that Yousef himself does not know?
options: Yousef placed his paper boat in the stream.
The water sparkled in the bright afternoon sun.
He watched it float away and hoped it would reach the sea.
He did not see the small rock waiting around the bend.
questions.why: The narrator knows about the rock even though Yousef cannot see it.

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: D

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Captain Saeed gripped the wheel as the waves grew taller. He was sure they could reach the harbor before dark. Below deck, young Hamad was certain the boat would sink, and he prayed quietly. The cook, meanwhile, thought only about whether the rice would spill.
questions.stem: How does the omniscient point of view help the reader understand the storm scene?
options: It shows how differently each person on the boat feels.
It keeps the reader guessing about what anyone is thinking.
It lets the captain tell his own story using I and me.
It shows only what the cook can see in the kitchen.
questions.why: We learn the captain's confidence, Hamad's fear and the cook's worry about rice.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: I watched my aunt add a pinch of something to the pot, but she hid the jar before I could read the label. I think it was saffron, but I'm not sure. She just winked at me.
questions.stem: What is one limit of the first-person narrator in the secret recipe passage?
options: The narrator cannot describe what the aunt does in the kitchen at all.
The narrator can't be sure what is in the jar or what the aunt thinks.
The narrator cannot tell the reader about personal feelings or wishes.
The narrator cannot use the word I to tell the story.
questions.why: A first-person narrator knows only what he or she sees and thinks.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Which point of view is each sentence written in?

rows.text: Nada knew she was right, and Sami knew he was wrong, but neither said a word.
Nada knew she was right, though she could only guess what Sami was thinking.
I knew I was right, but I said nothing.
You know you are right, so you smile and wait.

questions.why: Look at the pronouns and at whose thoughts are shared.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Layan carried the last box to the car. A moving truck was parked by the curb. Her eyes stung as she looked back at her old house. She remembered planting the lemon tree with her grandfather. She hoped her new room would feel like home someday.
questions.stem: Which two details best show that the moving day passage is told in third person limited from Layan's point of view? Choose two.
options: Layan carried the last box to the car.
A moving truck was parked by the curb.
She remembered planting the lemon tree with her grandfather.
She hoped her new room would feel like home someday.
questions.why: These details show Layan's private memories and hopes; the narrator shares no one else's.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: When the results were posted, Tariq searched the list for his name. It was not there. He turned away quickly so no one would see his face. He did not notice his friend Omar running toward him with good news: Tariq's poem had won a special prize.
questions.stem: What is the effect of the narrator sharing news that Tariq does not yet know?
options: The reader feels just as confused as Tariq does about the results.
The reader learns that Omar is the narrator of the story.
The reader understands that Tariq's poem lost the contest.
We know something Tariq doesn't, which builds hope and suspense.
questions.why: Because the reader knows about the prize, we wait eagerly for Tariq to find out.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: My cousin Fahad walked ahead of me on the trail. He looked tired, but maybe he was just thinking. I wished I knew what was on his mind. I decided to ask him at the next rest stop.
questions.stem: Select the two sentences that show the narrator cannot know what Fahad is thinking.

segments.text: My cousin Fahad walked ahead of me on the trail.
He looked tired, but maybe he was just thinking.
I wished I knew what was on his mind.
I decided to ask him at the next rest stop.

questions.why: The words maybe and I wished I knew show the narrator can only guess.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: A tall stranger knocked at the farmhouse door. Inside, Umm Khalid wondered who would visit so late. The stranger, cold and tired, hoped someone would offer him tea. Out in the barn, the old dog sensed something and began to bark.
questions.stem: Which point of view is used in the farmhouse passage, and how do you know?
options: third person limited, because the narrator follows only Umm Khalid inside
third person omniscient, because it shows what several characters think
first person, because the stranger tells about his own long trip
third person limited, because the narrator follows only the stranger
questions.why: We learn what Umm Khalid wonders, what the stranger hopes and what the dog senses.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: My twin brother, Saad, says he isn't scared of the dark. But every night, I see him leave the hallway light on.
questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence: The narrator learns about Saad's fear by ____.
options: reading Saad's mind
watching what Saad does
asking the reader questions
questions.why: A first-person narrator learns about others by watching them.

questions.passage: Every morning at seven, the clock tower rang across the square. Bilal, the baker, heard it and pulled the first loaves from the oven. questions.stem: Part A: What point of view is used in the clock tower passage?

options.label: A

options.label: B

options.label: D

options.text: Every morning at seven, the clock tower rang across the square.

options.label: C
options.text: Bilal, the baker, heard it and pulled the first loaves from the oven.

options.label: D
options.text: Across the street, Mrs. Mona heard it too.

questions.why: The narrator moves between characters and even knows the clockkeeper's secret.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: The room was silent except for pencils scratching. Rania stared at question five. She was sure she had studied this, but her mind felt empty. She glanced at the clock: ten minutes left.
questions.stem: How would the exam room passage most likely change if it were told in third person omniscient?
options: We might also learn how other students or the teacher feel.
The reader would learn much less about how Rania feels.
Rania would tell the story herself, using I and me.
The reader would be spoken to directly as you.
questions.why: An omniscient narrator can share the thoughts of anyone in the room.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: When Grandfather tells stories about the old days, my brother rolls his eyes. I think he is bored. But last night I saw him writing Grandfather's words in a notebook.
questions.stem: What does the last sentence of the grandfather passage show about the first-person narrator?
options: The narrator knows exactly what the brother is thinking all along.
The narrator is the grandfather telling the story.
The narrator does not care about the old stories.
The narrator's guess about the brother may have been wrong.
questions.why: The narrator thought the brother was bored, but his notebook shows he cares.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: You step into the cave, and the air turns cool. Your flashlight shows drawings of camels on the walls. You wonder who made them long ago.
questions.stem: Which two effects does the second-person point of view have in the cave passage? Choose two.
options: It makes the reader feel like part of the adventure.
It shows the thoughts of many different explorers.
It lets a character named Ali tell the story.
It places the reader inside the cave as the explorer.
questions.why: You puts the reader in the explorer's place.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text

rows.text: Waleed felt embarrassed.
The shopkeeper thought Waleed was being careless.
Waleed saw a shiny edge under the counter.
A woman in line secretly planned to help him.

questions.why: A limited narrator shares only Waleed's thoughts and what he notices.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Lulu woke before everyone else and tiptoed to the window. The street was quiet. She imagined the new dress waiting in her closet and the sweets she would share with her cousins. She could hardly wait for the day to begin.
questions.stem: Which statement best describes the narrator's point of view in the Eid morning passage?
options: Third person omniscient: the narrator shares the thoughts of the whole family.
First person: Lulu tells about her own morning using I.
Second person: the narrator tells the reader what to do on Eid.
Third person limited: the narrator shares only Lulu's thoughts and feelings.
questions.why: We learn what Lulu imagines and feels, and no one else's thoughts.

options.label: B

options.label: D

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: I ran into class out of breath. Ms. Asma looked at me with raised eyebrows. I was sure she was angry. Later, she told me she was only worried that I was sick.
questions.stem: What does the late-for-school passage show about a first-person narrator?
options: The narrator always knows exactly what the teacher is thinking.
The narrator can misread what other characters are feeling.
The narrator tells the story from outside the classroom.
The narrator speaks directly to the reader as you.
questions.why: The narrator thought Ms. Asma was angry, but she was worried.
