segments.text: Abeer picked up a glass camel for her mother.
She wondered if it was too expensive.
The shopkeeper hoped she would buy it soon, since it was nearly closing time.
Abeer counted her coins carefully.

questions.why: This sentence shows the shopkeeper's thoughts, not Abeer's.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Farmer Mansour looked up at the dark clouds and thanked God; his thirsty fields needed water. In the city, Dalia frowned at the same clouds, worried that her school's outdoor festival would be canceled.
questions.stem: Why might the author have chosen an omniscient narrator for the rain passage?
options: to keep the reader from knowing how Dalia feels about it
to let Farmer Mansour tell his own story about the rain
to give the reader directions about what to do in rain
to show how the same rain affects two people differently
questions.why: The narrator shows the farmer's joy and Dalia's worry about the same clouds.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Amal set out her date cookies and waited. Every few minutes, she checked whether anyone was coming. Her stomach fluttered each time someone walked past.
questions.stem: Choose the phrase that best completes the sentence: The narrator of the bake sale passage is limited to ____.
options: Amal's thoughts and feelings
every shopper's thoughts
the reader's own feelings
questions.why: We learn only how Amal feels as she waits.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Bandar slipped the apology note into Fahad's backpack before class. All morning, Fahad ignored him, and Bandar's hope sank lower with each hour. What Bandar did not know was that the note had fallen out in the hallway, where a cleaner swept it up with the dust.
questions.stem: What effect does the omniscient narrator's last sentence create in the apology note passage?
options: dramatic irony: readers know why Fahad is silent, but Bandar does not
suspense, because readers do not know where the note went at all
humor, because Fahad is only pretending to be angry with Bandar
confusion, because readers cannot tell which boy is speaking
questions.why: Readers know the note was lost, but Bandar does not.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Everyone knows I'm the best player on our team. Coach puts me on the bench sometimes, but that's only to give the others a chance. When we lost on Thursday, it was because the referee was unfair, not because I missed three shots.
questions.stem: Why should a reader be careful about trusting the first-person narrator of the basketball passage?
options: The narrator describes the game from outside the team, as a fan.
The narrator shares the thoughts of every player on the team.
He tells events in ways that always make himself look good.
The narrator speaks directly to the reader, calling the reader you.
questions.why: He blames the referee and ignores his own missed shots.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: At dinner, Uncle Hamad praised the soup loudly, though he secretly found it too salty. Aunt Latifa, who had made it, beamed with pride. Only young Dana noticed her uncle quietly drinking glass after glass of water, and she tried hard not to laugh.
questions.stem: How does the omniscient point of view create humor in the dinner passage?
options: It keeps every character's true feelings hidden from the reader.
It lets Aunt Latifa tell the whole story in her own words.
It reveals Uncle Hamad's secret opinion and Aunt Latifa's pride.
It speaks to the reader directly about how to cook a good soup.
questions.why: The reader knows the soup is salty while the cook feels proud.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Rashid trudged through the dunes, sure the oasis was just over the next hill. His water bottle was nearly empty. Each hill looked the same, but he told himself he was not lost.
questions.stem: Which two effects does the third person limited point of view create in the dunes passage? Choose two.
options: The reader shares Rashid's uncertainty about where he is.
Tension builds because the reader knows only what Rashid believes.
The reader learns exactly where the oasis is located.
The reader hears the thoughts of other travelers nearby.
questions.why: We stay inside Rashid's mind, so we do not know if he is lost either.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: You find the letter tucked inside an old book at the library. The paper is yellow, and the handwriting is shaky. You read the first line: “If you are reading this, the treasure is still hidden.” You look around. No one is watching.
questions.stem: What is the main effect of the second-person point of view in the letter passage?
options: It pulls the reader into the mystery as the finder of the letter.
It shows the reader the private thoughts of the letter's writer.
It helps the narrator explain events from long ago.
It makes the reader an outside observer watching the scene.
questions.why: Using you makes the reader feel like the one holding the letter.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: A writer wants to tell a story about a school play. Which point of view best fits each goal?

rows.text: Show what every actor is secretly worried about.
Let the reader feel like the actor on the stage.
Have the lead actor tell her own experience.
Keep the reader inside one actor's mind only.

questions.why: Each point of view gives the reader a different kind of view into the story.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: The kite fluttered in the branches of the acacia tree. Sami, who had lost it, had already given up and gone home sad. Across the road, his neighbor Rayan spotted the kite and decided to climb up for it, planning to return it in the morning.
questions.stem: How would the reader's experience of the kite passage change if it were told in third person limited from Sami's point of view?
options: The reader would learn even more about Rayan's thoughts and plans.
The reader would be told what the kite itself is thinking.
Nothing would change, because Sami already knows about the plan.
We would not learn Rayan's plan, so the kite would seem lost for good.
questions.why: Sami does not know Rayan's plan, so a limited narrator could not tell it.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: When my name was called, I walked to the stage and tried to look calm. My knees felt like jelly. I looked out at the audience, and I could not find my mother's face. I told myself she must be stuck in traffic.
questions.stem: Which statement best explains how the first-person point of view shapes the award passage?
options: Readers learn exactly why the mother is not in the audience.
Readers see the whole event through the mother's eyes instead.
We feel the narrator's nerves but cannot know where the mother is.
Readers are told what each person in the audience is thinking.
questions.why: We know only what the narrator sees and feels on stage.

questions.stem: Choose the term that completes the sentence: Because readers know about the cake while Mona does not, the passage creates ____.
options: a flashback
dramatic irony
a simile
questions.why: Dramatic irony happens when readers know something a character does not.

partA.stem: Part A: Which point of view is used in the desert guide passage?

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Jumana opened the box slowly. Inside was the watch her grandfather used to wear. Her throat tightened.

options: I opened the box slowly. Inside was the watch my grandfather used to wear. My throat tightened.

Jumana opened the box slowly. Inside was the watch I used to wear. Her throat tightened.
She opened the box slowly. Inside was the watch her grandfather used to wear. Her throat tightened.
questions.why: First person replaces Jumana and her with I and my throughout.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Waleed was certain that Khalid had tripped him on purpose during the race. He refused to shake Khalid's hand afterward. Khalid walked away confused, still rubbing the ankle he had twisted when he stumbled into Waleed.
questions.stem: How does the narrator's knowledge of both boys affect the reader's view of the conflict after the race?
options: Readers agree with Waleed that Khalid cheated on purpose in the race.
Readers cannot tell what either of the two boys thinks or feels.
Readers see the trip was an accident, so Waleed's anger is mistaken.
Readers learn the story only from inside Khalid's own thoughts.
questions.why: Knowing Khalid twisted his ankle shows the fall was not on purpose.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Asma told her best friend that she was moving to Dammam. Her friend promised to keep it secret. That evening, the friend told no one, though she felt so sad that she cried in her room for an hour. Asma, at home, wondered whether she had been wise to tell.
questions.stem: Select the two sentences that show the narrator moving between the minds of different characters.

segments.text: Asma told her best friend that she was moving to Dammam.
Her friend promised to keep it secret.
That evening, the friend told no one, though she felt so sad that she cried in her room for an hour.
Asma, at home, wondered whether she had been wise to tell.

questions.why: One sentence shows the friend's private sadness, and the other shows Asma's private doubt.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Our neighbor, old Mr. Jaber, never smiles. He sits on his porch and stares at the street. My friends say he dislikes children. But yesterday, when my ball rolled into his yard, he picked it up and gently tossed it back.
questions.stem: What does the first-person point of view suggest about the narrator's understanding of Mr. Jaber?
options: The narrator fully understands Mr. Jaber's private thoughts and plans.
The narrator is Mr. Jaber himself, describing his own quiet life.
The narrator proves that Mr. Jaber truly dislikes all children.
The narrator relies on rumors and actions, so the view may be incomplete.
questions.why: The narrator only sees what Mr. Jaber does and hears what friends say.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.stem: Which two statements about point of view are accurate? Choose two.
options: A third person limited narrator shares only one character's inner thoughts.
A second-person narrator always tells the thoughts of every character.
A third person omniscient narrator must be a character in the story.
A first-person narrator can be mistaken about other characters' feelings.
questions.why: Limited stays with one mind, and a first-person narrator can misjudge others.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Bushra sat in the waiting room, staring at the doors. Every time a nurse walked out, her heart jumped. Nobody told her anything about her grandmother. She counted the tiles on the floor to stay calm.
questions.stem: The author tells the waiting room scene only through Bushra's eyes. What is the most likely reason?
options: to explain exactly what the doctors are doing behind the doors
to show what each nurse thinks about the girl waiting
to teach the reader the rules for visiting a hospital
to make the reader share Bushra's worry and uncertainty
questions.why: Like Bushra, the reader does not know what is happening behind the doors.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Hamza told his little sister that her drawing was the best he had ever seen. He did not really think so, but he could not bear to see her disappointed. His sister ran to hang it on the fridge, glowing.
questions.stem: Which point of view is used in the drawing passage, and what does it allow the reader to see?
options: third person omniscient; it shows the thoughts of the whole family
third person limited; it reveals what Hamza really thinks
first person; it lets the little sister explain her drawing
second person; it tells the reader how to praise a drawing
questions.why: We learn only Hamza's private thoughts; his sister is described from outside.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: Faris stepped onto the narrow bridge. He told himself not to look down. Behind him, his cousin Mazen hoped Faris would turn back, but he said nothing.
questions.stem: True or false: The bridge passage stays in third person limited from Faris's point of view the whole time.
questions.why: The last sentence shares Mazen's hope, so the narrator leaves Faris's mind.

questions.mapArea: Literary Text
questions.passage: As the lanterns rose into the night sky, each person on the beach made a quiet wish. Old Ibrahim wished for rain on his farm. Little Sara wished for a puppy. Her mother wished only that her children would always be this happy.
questions.stem: What is the overall effect of the omniscient narration in the lantern passage?
options: It connects many different hopes into one shared, peaceful moment.
It creates suspense by hiding what each of the characters wants.
It shows that only one person on the beach made a wish.
It makes the reader the main character of the scene.
questions.why: The narrator shares each person's wish, joining them in one scene.
